title: Scientists Are Stumped by This Strange Object in Space
summary: The rocky body called 1998 KY26 is moving in ways that gravity alone cannot explain. So far, no one knows why.

It’s small, it’s fast, and nobody is entirely sure what it is.


In the simplest terms, the object called 1998 KY26 is a boulder orbiting the sun, measuring about 36 feet across. But it is moving in a way that cannot be explained by gravity alone. That has led to a debate about whether it’s a comet, an asteroid or something else entirely.


No, it’s not an alien spaceship. Nor is it likely to be a lost Soviet spacecraft.


Discovered in 1998 by[Tom Gehrels](https://www.nytimes.com/1996/07/28/magazine/the-asteroids-are-coming-the-asteroids-are-coming.html) , an astronomer at the University of Arizona, 1998 KY26 at first appeared to be an asteroid. But its idiosyncratic accelerations cause it to stray from the neat orbit suggested by Johannes Kepler’s laws of planetary motion, which have been taught to generations of physics students. The deviations are tiny, but they are meaningful.


One idea was that 1998 KY26 was a “[dark comet](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2406424121) ” — one that simply lacked the signature tail composed of dust particles released as the sun caused buried ice to vaporize. This process, called sublimation, can look like 1998 KY26’s acceleration.


A new paper published in the scientific journal Icarus[has deepened the mystery](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103526004276?via%3Dihub) by arguing that the average temperature of 1998 KY26, a balmy minus 53 degrees Fahrenheit, is “far above” the threshold for ice.


“If something has ice, then it’s a comet,” said Darryl Z. Seligman, an assistant professor of physics and astronomy at Michigan State University who had been a leading proponent of the “dark comet” hypothesis. But no ice meant no comet. “The surface of KY26 is too warm,” Dr. Seligman said in an interview. So there went one of the simpler explanations.


Dr. Seligman added that while we have the tools to peer into deep space, near-Earth objects present a scientific challenge of their own. “There’s not tons of data on very near-Earth objects. They’re super small and faint,” he said.
